newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia rethinks its approach to industry.
newsitem.headline: Croatia rethinks its approach to industry.

text.p: Croatia plans a radical revamp of its industrial policy aimed at helping state-owned companies develop and modernise, Economy Minister Nenad Porges said in an interview with Reuters.

The new approach follows a period of war during which the government supported industrial firms without any regard to the cost. A number, including troubled shipyards and metal giant Djuro Djakovic, were nationalised in 1991 because their activities were considered vital to the country's defence.

"We are committed to industrial development and incentives to boost industrial output," said Porges, who is responsible for energy and trade as well as industry. "The idea is for key branches to keep their comparative advantages and develop them further. But technological modernisation is vital."
He said it could be some time before state-owned firms were ready for sale to the private sector.
Industry's contribution to Croatia's gross domestic product (GDP) is estimated at some 20 percent, with energy and trade accounting for a further 15 percent.
Industrial output is staging a modest but steady recovery after plunging as a result of devastation and loss of markets during the 1991-95 conflict in former Yugoslavia.
Output rose by 3.7 percent in January-April this year compared with the same period of 1996.
After nationalisation, the government appointed state officials to supervise management of the companies and has since given them considerable cash injections to keep them afloat.
It also took over their debts to the banking sector when it began overhauling four leading banks. Porges declined to give any figures, but implied that expenditure had been vast.
He said the shipbuilding industry, which was teetering on the brink of collapse four years ago, would be kept busy through 1999 by what he described as foreign "mega projects".
These orders were obtained with government help and backed up by its guarantees, making it possible for the five state-owned yards to rake in $430 million in 1996.
Now the ministry has a new plan for amalgamating four yards -- in Pula, Rijeka, Trogir and Split -- to combine parts of their production capacities and boost their profitability.

The yard in Kraljevica on the northern Adriatic has the best prospects for continuing on its own and may be the only one to be offered eventually to private investors, the minister said without committing himself to any time frame.
"It is a proud thing that Croatian vessels are plying routes such as the Stockholm-Helsinki line," he said, "but we should ask ourselves whether it is worth the taxpayers' money."
Another project in the pipeline aims to revitalise the country's largest steel mill in Sisak, for which the government failed to find any investors in a tender last year.
Porges also mentioned plans to spur the chemical industry, pharmaceuticals and parts of machinery production which have a strong export tradition.

"(Electrical equipment manufacturer) Koncar is fit to get subcontracting jobs on energy projects in Asian and South American countries...Djuro Djakovic has managed to restructure largely thanks to its own efforts and could also make a return to the market," Porges said.
